pages.x: Around 1299 Osman, leader of a small Turkish band on the edge of Byzantine lands in Anatolia, began raiding and taking the towns around him. A later legend says he dreamed of a tree growing from his body whose branches spread over the whole world.

His son Orhan took Bursa in 1326 and made it his capital. In 1354 an earthquake shattered the walls of Gallipoli, and the Ottomans crossed into Europe. In 1389 they beat the Serbs at Kosovo, though Sultan Murad I was killed there.

Sultan Bayezid I, called the Thunderbolt, conquered fast until 1402, when Timur, the conqueror from Central Asia, crushed his army at Ankara and took him prisoner. Legend says Timur carried him about in an iron cage. Bayezid died a captive, and his sons fought each other for ten years.
The empire recovered, and in 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople and made it his capital. The sultans now saw themselves as the heirs of Rome.
The sultans' best troops were the janissaries, Christian boys taken from Balkan villages, made Muslims and trained from childhood as soldiers loyal only to the sultan.
pages.fx: They were one of the first standing armies in Europe, armed with guns, and the terror of their enemies for two centuries.

pages.x: Selim I, called the Grim, crushed the Safavids of Persia at Chaldiran in 1514, and in 1516 and 1517 conquered the Mamluk lands of Syria and Egypt. With Mecca and Medina, he took the title of protector of the holy cities.

His son Suleiman the Magnificent took Belgrade, destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács in 1526, where the young Hungarian king died, and in 1529 besieged Vienna. Snow, rain and stubborn defenders drove him back. Vienna would stop the Ottomans again in 1683.

The Ottoman Empire lasted more than 600 years, until 1922, ruling peoples of many faiths and languages from Algeria to Iraq and from Hungary to Yemen. Modern Turkey grew out of it, and its food, music and buildings shaped the whole region.
